props.title: Taking Sides

sections.content: Taking Sides dives deep into the morally murky waters of art's relationship with politics through the denazification trial of conductor Wilhelm Furtwängler. Like The Last Metro (1980) and The Pianist (2002), it grapples with the complex choices artists faced under Nazi rule. Director István Szabó, who explored similar themes in Mephisto (1981), crafts a devastating chamber drama that asks whether great art can justify moral compromise.

sections.content: The film's interrogation scenes between Keitel's Major Steve Arnold and Stellan Skarsgård's Furtwängler echo other powerful post-war confrontations like those in Judgment at Nuremberg (1961) and The Reader (2008). These tense exchanges expose the impossible choices faced by those living under totalitarian regimes, similar to themes explored in The Lives of Others (2006) and Good (2008).

Szabó's direction particularly shines in how he uses musical sequences, letting Furtwängler's conducting of Beethoven and Bruckner speak to both his genius and his potential complicity. This approach recalls Amadeus (1984) and Immortal Beloved (1994) in how it weaves classical music into the dramatic narrative while examining the personal costs of artistic pursuit. sections.content: The film connects to a broader cinematic examination of artists under oppression, from Death and the Maiden (1994) to Music Box (1989). These works all wrestle with questions of cultural preservation versus moral compromise. The Conformist (1970) and The Garden of the Finzi-Continis (1970) similarly explore how intellectuals and artists navigated fascism's rise.
